newsitem.title: FRANCE: French shares end weaker, Jospin speech awaited.
newsitem.headline: French shares end weaker, Jospin speech awaited.

text.p: French shares closed weaker after a day of relatively light trading on Wednesday amid investor caution ahead of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's debut parliamentary policy speech on Thursday.

The CAC-40 blue-chip index ended down 0.39 percent, or 10.86 points, at 2,751, after shedding more than one percent earlier in the day. The CAC-40 futures contract finished three points down at 2,748. Stock market volume was 7.1 billion francs.

Analysts say it is unclear whether Jospin can elaborate significantly on economic policy and privatisations after just two weeks in government and ahead of an audit of state finances which is expected to be completed around mid-July.

Jospin, who is due to speak to the National Assembly from 1500 GMT on Thursday, is under pressure to deliver on promises that jobs and work time cuts take priority over austerity and amid demands to raise the minimum wage and reopen talks on public sector pay.

Shares in drinks and luxury goods group LVMH finished 1.7 percent lower, recovering somewhat from heavy opening losses after announcing on Tuesday that it had bought 0.23 percent of Grand Metropolitan.

It says it is not planning to make an offer and declined to elaborate on Wednesday. Analysts believe it it manoeuvering to defend its drinks links with Guinness after Guinness and Grand Met's recent merger announcement.

Appliance maker Moulinex reported a 1996/97 net attributable profit of 29 million francs, its first full-year profit since 1991. It had a 702 million franc loss in 1995/96 after taking a 600 million restructuring charge.
It said it expected a significant rise in operating profit and return on capital for the 1997/98 year after an increase in operating profit to 160 million from 54 million in 1996/97.

Skis Rossignol sports equipment company's stock closed sharply up despite a 34.2 percent drop in 1996/97 profit to 76.1 million francs. Investors responded well to a relatively robust operating profit and saw provisions as a sing of a clean-up, fund managers said.

Investment certificates in the Credit Lyonnais state-owned bank were a major gainer, closing 6.99 percent higher. Leven brokerage was cited as switching to a buy recommendation on the non-voting stock.
Oil group Total, industrial giant Alcatel and electronics group Schneider ended weaker, with the share slides attributed by traders to profit-taking.
